result.summary: After the war, Thebes burns its dead while Creon forbids burial of the Argives. Argia and Antigone secretly cremate Polynices, and the Argive widows win Theseus' help at Athens. Theseus marches on Thebes, kills Creon, and the poem closes with the poet's farewell to his Thebaid.

scenes.title: Thebes mourns on the battlefield
scenes.summary: The Thebans emerge fearfully and search the field for their dead. They burn them on pyres, with Menoeceus honoured above all.
scenes.stakes: The grieving Thebans fear the battlefield and the dead, and the Argive dead go unburied.

scenes.title: Creon's grief and decree
scenes.summary: Creon laments Menoeceus and forbids anyone to burn the Argive dead, on pain of death.
scenes.stakes: Anyone who gives the Argives fire will be put to death.

scenes.title: The widows learn of the ban
scenes.summary: The Argive women march toward Thebes. Ornytus warns them of Creon's decree, and Argia resolves to go on alone.
scenes.stakes: Argia risks death at Creon's hands to bury her husband.

scenes.title: Argia finds Polynices
scenes.summary: Argia crosses the dark country to the battlefield. Juno has the Moon light the plain, and Argia finds Polynices' body.
scenes.stakes: Argia faces Creon's guards and execution.

scenes.title: Antigone and the double flame
scenes.summary: Antigone arrives and the two women wash and burn Polynices on Eteocles' pyre. The flame splits in two and they are seized by guards.
scenes.stakes: They face death for defying Creon's decree.

scenes.title: Suppliants at the Altar of Clemency
scenes.summary: Juno leads the Argive women to Athens. Theseus returns in triumph and Capaneus' wife begs him to compel burial.
scenes.stakes: The Argive dead remain unburied unless Athens helps.

scenes.title: Theseus marches on Thebes
scenes.summary: Theseus answers the plea and sends Phegeus with a challenge to Creon. The Attic host assembles and marches.
scenes.stakes: Theseus risks war with Thebes to uphold burial rights.

scenes.title: Theseus kills Creon
scenes.summary: Phegeus' threat shakes Creon. In battle Theseus routs the Thebans and kills Creon, then peace is made and the burials proceed.
scenes.stakes: Creon fights for his life and the city.

scenes.title: The poet's farewell
scenes.summary: Statius addresses his finished poem, hoping it will endure and follow the Aeneid.

alias_notes.explanation: Juno is called Saturnia as the daughter of Saturn.
A title of Pallas, linked to Lake Triton.

notable_quotes.reason: Ornytus' bitter verdict on Creon's character.
Statius bids his poem revere the Aeneid and follow it from afar.

analysis.text: The book contrasts Creon's cruelty in refusing burial with Athens' altar of Clemency, framing burial as a law of gods and humanity.
The closing address shows Statius' hope for his poem after twelve years of work, and mentions the emperor's favour and its place beside Virgil.

legacy.text: The altar of Clemency and Theseus' intervention echo the Athenian tradition of defending the right to burial, as in Euripides' Suppliants.

fun_facts.text: Statius says he worked twelve years on the Thebaid, matching the Aeneid's twelve books.

language_notes.text: Tithonia is Aurora, goddess of dawn, named for her husband Tithonus. She drives away the clouds before Phoebus the sun rises.
Dircean means Theban, from the spring of Dirce near Thebes.
Idalian birds are doves, sacred to Venus, whose cult was centred at Idalium in Cyprus.
The ravished augur is Amphiaraus, swallowed alive by a chasm in the earth. The enemy of the gods is Capaneus, struck by Jove's lightning.
Ogygian means Theban, from Ogyges, a legendary early king of Thebes.
Creon, now ruling, forbids burial of Polynices, Eteocles' brother, who attacked Thebes with the Argives. So he is treated as an Argive.
The Tirynthian is Hercules, who burned himself on a pyre on Mount Oeta and was taken up to the stars.
Pelasgian is used for Argive/Greek; the Argive army is meant, not an ancient tribe specifically.
Echion's city is Thebes; Echion was one of the Sown Men who sprang from the dragon's teeth and founded its noble families.
Fanes are temples or sacred places.
Creon says he cannot mingle Argos and Mycenae with his son's ashes as a worthy offering, since he owes his throne to the boy's death.
The dread brothers are Eteocles and Polynices, who killed each other; Tartarus is the underworld's place of the dead.
Oedipus, father of the dead brothers, also lost his sons; Creon compares his own loss to Oedipus's.
Lernaean means Argive, from Lerna, a marsh near Argos; Erebus is the dark underworld.
"Fill up the tale of corpses" means to add to the count of the dead.
Inachian means Argive, from Inachus, the legendary river-god and first king of Argos.
Argia is Polynices' wife and daughter of Adrastus, king of Argos; Mycenae stands here for her Argive home, which she would abandon.
Tydeus' 'crime and impious gnawing': dying, he gnawed the head of his enemy Melanippus, a horror that appalled even Minerva.
The seer is Amphiaraus, swallowed alive by the earth, so his wife Eriphyle, who betrayed him for a necklace, builds a pyre with no body.
Maenalian Diana's comrade is Atalanta, mother of Parthenopaeus; Evadne is wife of Capaneus, killed by Jove's thunderbolt.
The Theban mother is Ino, who became the sea-goddess Leucothea, honoured at the Isthmus; the Eleusinian is Ceres, whose torches guide the women.
The Saturnian is Juno, daughter of Saturn, who protects the Argive women.
Busiris, an Egyptian king, sacrificed strangers; the Odrysian stall refers to Diomedes' man-eating horses of Thrace; Sicilian deities allude to cruel rites.
Theseus of Athens (Cecropian) had just campaigned against the Amazons by the Thermodon, and later compels Creon to allow burial.
Rhodope and Phasis are regions associated with Amazons and fierce maidens; not even they would dare defy Creon's law.
Menoetes is Argia's old attendant, her guardian since girlhood.
Refers to a frenzied votary of Cybele at her Phrygian rites on Mount Dindymus; the priestess is chosen by the goddess and wears a wool-bound wreath.
"Father Titan" is the Sun (Hyperion's son), whose chariot sinks in the western (Hesperian) sea at evening.
"Ogygian" means Theban, from Ogyges, a legendary early king of Thebes; "sepulture" means burial.
Ceres searched the world for her daughter Persephone, carried off by Pluto, the "dark ravisher"; she lit torches at Aetna's fires.
Juno alludes to the triple-length night when Jove conceived Hercules, in which Cynthia (the Moon) was made to serve; Juno breaks off bitterly.
"Cynthia" is a name of the Moon goddess, Diana, from Mount Cynthus.
"Saturnia" means Juno, daughter of Saturn.
"Were lies" is the translator's odd rendering; Argia is asking whether the robber (Eteocles) lay in wait for Polynices.
Argia vows Polynices will not lack funeral fire; the "little Polynices" is the son she hopes to bear or has borne, to tend his memory.
"Cadmean" means Theban, from Cadmus, the legendary founder of Thebes; here it refers to Antigone.
"Stolen mourning" means grief performed in secret, against Creon's ban on burying Polynices.
Phaëthon, son of Hyperion (the Sun), crashed his father's chariot and fell into the Padus (Po). His sisters wept until they became poplars, or a 'weeping grove'.
"The Fury had spared the fires for mutual strife" means the Fury kept this pyre unburnt so the brothers' hatred could continue.
Orcus is the underworld; the Eumenides are the Furies. The comparison evokes infernal fire locked in conflict.
"Ever debarred from justice" refers to Polynices, who was denied his share of rule and now denied burial rites.
Phoronean dames: Argive women, from Phoroneus, legendary early king of Argos. Pallas is Minerva (Athena), Athens' patron goddess.
Erechthean means Athenian, after Erechtheus, an early legendary king of Athens.
Ogygian means Theban, from Ogyges, a legendary early king associated with Thebes.
Refers to Procne and Philomela, transformed into birds after Tereus, king of Thrace (Getic land), wronged Philomela. Their cries are the 'mutilated speech', since her tongue was cut out.
The gods gave Athens laws, a 'new man' and sacred rites. The seeds are grain, given by Ceres, who taught Athens agriculture.
Examples of refuge: Oedipus's rage was checked, Olynthus's killer was sheltered, and Orestes was defended from the Furies of his mother Clytemnestra.
Baldricks are ornamental belts worn across the chest; targes are light shields; Maeotis is the Sea of Azov.
Son of Aegeus is Theseus. The 'sevenfold host' is the seven chieftains' army against Thebes, city of Agenor's line.
Creon is likened to Pluto ('father of the Furies') and Charon, the ferryman, who bar the dead from the underworld; unburied souls wander.
Cecrops was legendary first king of Athens; 'sons of Cecrops' means the Athenians. Emathians and Thracians stand for northern Greeks whose dead lie unburied.
Sinis, Cercyon and Sciron were brigands Theseus killed on his road to Athens. The speaker says he spared such men's bodies, so he should not deny Argive dead burial.
'Ween' is archaic for 'think' or 'suppose'. Tanais is the river Don, here standing for the Amazons' homeland.
'Thoughtest thou' is archaic second-person verb form: 'Did you think'. Theseus rebukes Creon for assuming he was beaten.
Tritonia is Pallas Athena. The 'Libyan terror' is the Gorgon Medusa's head on her aegis, whose snakes come alive.
Aegeus, Theseus' father, threw himself into the sea on seeing black sails, wrongly believing his son dead; the Aegean is named for him.
Boreas, the Thracian north wind, carried off Orithyia from the Ilissus (Elisos); the river is said to have hidden him.
The hill is the Athenian Acropolis, where Pallas and Neptune contested for the city; her gift was the olive tree.
The Gnosian maid is Ariadne of Cnossos, who gave Theseus the thread to escape the Minotaur's labyrinth.
Antigone and Argia (Adrastus' daughter, widow of Polynices) are being led to death for defying Creon's ban on burying the Argive dead.
Tyrian hills: Thebes is called Tyrian because its founder Cadmus came from Tyre in Phoenicia.
Pelasgians: here a poetic name for the Argives, the Greeks who attacked Thebes.
Sarcastic, bitter question: the poet says Creon spared the old corpse-strewn ground only to choose fresh ground for more slaughter.
Bellona is the Roman goddess of war.
Cecropian means Athenian, from Cecrops, legendary first king of Athens.
Theseus' Marathonian shaft recalls his deeds near Marathon; 'born of the main' hints that Neptune was said to be his father.
Mavors is Mars; Edonian and Haemus refer to Thrace, his homeland; sons of Agenor are Thebans.
Tartarus is the deepest region of the underworld, where the wicked are punished.
Thyrsus is Bacchus' ivy-wreathed staff; the Ganges reference recalls Bacchus' conquest of India.
Thyiads are Bacchus' frenzied women worshippers.
Evadne threw herself on Capaneus' pyre; the Arcadian is Parthenopaeus, whose mother is Atalanta of Erymanthus's region.
The Aeneid is Virgil's epic, the model Statius humbly asks his poem to follow.

context_notes.text: Teumesus and Cithaeron are hills near Thebes. Cithaeron was also tied to Theban myth, including the death of Pentheus.
Menoeceus, son of Creon, sacrificed himself for Thebes by leaping from the walls, after the seer Tiresias said this would bring victory.
Menoeceus, Creon's son, killed himself on Thebes' walls to fulfil a prophecy that his death would give Thebes victory.
Creon became king only because Eteocles died; he is bitterly aware that his son's death brought him the throne.
Refusing burial to the Argive dead is the decree that leads to the Argive women's appeal to Athens and Theseus.
After the failed expedition of the Seven against Thebes, Creon forbids burial of the Argive dead; their widows set out to claim the bodies.
Iris is the messenger goddess; preserving the corpses with divine ointments is a miraculous aid sent by Juno.
Creon has posted guards over the unburied dead; denial of burial barred the soul's rest in Greek belief.
Marathonian arms means Athenian forces; Ogygian means Theban, from the legendary early king Ogyges.
Argia, wife of Polynices, is going to Thebes to find his unburied body; Creon has forbidden burial of the Argive dead. Menoetes is her escort.
Creon, ruler of Thebes after the brothers' deaths, forbade burial of the Argive dead, so Argia must hide her torch.
Juno favours Argos and is heading to Athens to persuade Theseus to help the suppliant Argive women.
Polynices married Argia, daughter of King Adrastus of Argos, and led the Argive army against Thebes to claim the throne from his brother Eteocles.
Menoetes is the old attendant who guards Antigone and has stayed near Polynices' body.
Argia, daughter of Adrastus king of Argos, is Polynices' wife. Creon of Thebes has forbidden burial of the Argive dead.
Eteocles and Polynices killed each other in single combat; the brothers' hatred was so great that their flame divides.
The Altar of Clemency (Mercy) was a real Athenian cult, a refuge for suppliants, unusual in being dedicated to an abstract virtue.
Theseus, king of Athens, returns from defeating the Amazons, whom Statius calls Scythian, and brings back their queen Hippolyte as his bride.
Capaneus' wife is Evadne, who speaks for the Argive widows. Capaneus was one of the seven champions killed at Thebes.
The speaker is the Argive widow pleading for burial of the dead. Theseus is called Neptunian because Neptune was reputed to be his father.
Tyrian towers means Thebes, founded by Cadmus from Tyre. Danai are the Argives, whose dead Creon forbids burying.
Hippolyte is the Amazon queen whom Theseus married; her unborn child would be Hippolytus.
Theseus' shield shows his capture of the Cretan bull and the Minotaur's labyrinth, his early exploits.
Phegeus is Theseus' envoy, carrying an olive branch, the traditional sign of peaceful embassy.
Statius says the Thebaid took twelve years to write, matching its twelve books.
Caesar here means the emperor Domitian, Statius' patron.

literary_notes.text: The Thebans' disbelief at their safety is compared to sailors unsteady on land after a long voyage.
Doves frightened by a vanished snake mirror the Thebans, who still fear the enemy after the retreat.
Feasting on sorrow turns grief into food, showing how the mourners cling to their lamentation.
Likening Menoeceus' pyre to that of Hercules elevates him to heroic, near-divine status.
Creon says honor-seeking cost his son the throne, yet the son's sacrifice is what actually gave Creon the kingship.
Creon's sudden address to Jove turns private grief into a cry against the gods.
Sceptre and crown stand for kingship; offering them to the dead shows he values them less than his son.
His wish to revive the corpses just to feed them to beasts shows grief hardening into cruelty.
The widows are compared to a captive throng, picturing their grief and helplessness as a kind of enslavement.
Hecate, Ino and Ceres join the women's grief, making the divine world share their mourning.
Ornytus implies Creon's humanity can only be taught by force, bitterly contrasting the king's name for justice with his cruelty.
Ornytus' warning is likened to a tigress's roar frightening heifers; the women become helpless prey, each dreading being chosen.
Memories of Polynices shift from wedding to departure to bloodied corpse, showing love darkening into obsession with burial.
Argia thanks Ornytus for cheering her, though his warning was meant to deter her; his words only spur her on.
Argia's fearless desperation is compared to a frenzied priestess of Cybele, making her seem possessed and dangerous.
The narrator's exclamation generalizes her endurance, commenting directly on the power of love and grief.
Argia addresses the city of Thebes as a person, bargaining with it for her husband's body.
Ceres' desperate search for Persephone mirrors Argia's search for her husband, elevating her grief to myth.
Shadows start in terror and stars lose their radiance, as nature itself reacts to the Moon's sudden brilliance.
She recognizes the cloak she herself wove, now stained with blood, a painful turn of her own loving work.
Her vow of burning and tending the tomb anticipates the funeral rites to follow, and the rivalry with Creon's decree.
Antigone's escape is compared to a lioness bursting out, showing her fierce, long-restrained fury.
Each woman fears the other as a possible enemy, though the reader knows both are mourners; the misunderstanding is soon resolved.
The pyre's flame splitting in two embodies the brothers' undying hatred, continuing even after death.
Hatred is described as 'alive' in the flames, as if the emotion itself survived the brothers' bodies.
The women compete to claim guilt, showing their courage and devotion, even a longing for death.
The narrator voices the crowd's bewilderment, making the reader share the Athenians' puzzlement at the sudden throng.
The mourners' lamentation is compared to the mythic birds' cries, linking the Argive women's grief to older stories of wrong.
The absence of any statue shows Clemency as an inner feeling rather than an idol, dwelling in human hearts.
Cranes arriving in warmth from northern storms are compared to the women finding relief at the altar.
Stressing the dead men's shared humanity, the widow appeals to Theseus' sympathy and makes Creon's denial seem monstrous.
She turns abruptly to address Athens directly, intensifying her plea and pressing the city to live up to its reputation.
Dawn, the pole, birds and beasts all recoil from the corpses, showing how monstrous Creon's refusal of burial is.
Theseus' renewed vigor is compared to a wounded bull hiding his hurts in dust when a rival bellows.
Gods, nature and the dead are set against Thebes' Furies, framing the war as justice versus impiety.
The army's advance is likened to Jupiter's winter storm, with mountains, waves and lightning conveying overwhelming force.
The shield's imagery of the bull and labyrinth embodies Theseus' heroic past and terrifies his enemies.
The narrator cries out to the 'fatal day', voicing grief at peace lost after so much bloodshed.
Wavering Athenian ardour is compared to winds weakening without forests, and waves quiet without a shore.
Theseus' spear is likened to Mars driving his chariot down from the mountain with Death and Panic, magnifying his terror.
Dogs and wolves preying on the cowering contrast with lions, whose strength is anger; Theseus is the lion.
The mail's fine iron mesh and spurting blood give a vivid, grim picture of Creon's death.
Theseus turns Creon's own refusal to bury the dead against him by promising him burial.
The poet's long work is a little ship that has voyaged far and now deserves harbour.
Statius addresses his finished poem directly, personifying it as a living thing that must outlive him.
